extracted.intended_audience: telecommunications industry stakeholders, state and local emergency communications officials, FCC rulemaking commenters, and attorneys/practitioners who participate in notice-and-comment proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural rules for the Federal Communications Commission's use of a direct final rule to repeal obsolete rules, including standards for when prior notice-and-comment may be forborne, how the direct final rule process is conducted, and filing/approval requirements for related State EAS plans and certifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause to forgo notice and comment (APA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), an agency may for good cause find that notice and public comment 'are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest' and thus need not follow notice-and-comment procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior notice and comment are 'unnecessary' when 'the administrative rule is a routine determination, insignificant in nature and impact, and inconsequential to the industry and to the public.' The Commission applies a 'good cause' analysis to determine whether prior notice and comment can be forgone; this analysis is the statutory predicate for using direct final rule procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for identifying rules appropriate for repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that 'plainly no longer serve the public interest' are candidates for repeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of such rules include those that: (a) have sunset by operation of law (e.g., 47 CFR 9.20), (b) govern an expired event or compliance deadline (e.g., §4.17(e), §9.11(a), §9.19(d)(1), various §10 and §11 deadlines), (c) regulate obsolete technology (e.g., §11.16 procedures for priority-based processing no longer followed), (d) are no longer used in practice by the FCC or licensees (e.g., voluntary EAS participation procedures in §11.11(e), §11.43), and (e) are duplicative, outdated, unnecessary, unlawful, anticompetitive, or otherwise not in the public interest (e.g., references to bodies that no longer exist such as the JTRB). The Commission may rely on these categories when concluding prior notice and comment is unnecessary for repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct Final Rule process and timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: When employing a direct final rule process, the Commission will adopt rule changes without prior notice and comment but will provide an opportunity for public comment and follow a compressed procedural timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission will publish the item in the Federal Register and allow for comment from interested parties within 20 days of Federal Register publication; until 20 days after publication, the proceeding is 'permit-but-disclose' for ex parte rules. Filings addressing the rule changes are prohibited more than 20 days after Federal Register publication absent further direction. The direct final rules will be effective 60 days after Federal Register publication unless significant adverse comments are received. If significant adverse comments are received, the Bureau will publish a timely withdrawal so that the rule change does not become effective until any additional procedures have been followed. If significant adverse comments concern only a subset of the revisions, the Bureau will withdraw only those portions. If no comments are filed, the rule changes take effect as specified (no separate confirmation anticipated). If comments are filed but none are significant adverse, the Bureau may issue a Public Notice explaining why the comments were not significant adverse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and treatment of 'significant adverse comment'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission adopts the ACUS formulation that a comment should be considered a 'significant adverse comment' if it explains why: (a) the [direct final] rule would be inappropriate, including challenges to the rule's underlying premise or approach; or (b) the [direct final] rule would be ineffective or unacceptable without a change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The touchstone for the Commission's analysis is whether the comment materially calls into question the conclusion that prior notice and comment is unnecessary under the APA. While the ACUS formulation is a useful guide, the Commission's statutory determination of 'good cause' to forgo notice and comment remains the critical issue. Where significant adverse comments are found, affected rule changes will be withdrawn and not made effective until further procedures are completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment filing procedures and formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructions for submitting comments on the direct final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments must be filed in GN Docket No. 25-133. Electronic filers should use the Commission's Electronic Comment Filing System (ECFS) at https://www.fcc.gov/ecfs/. Paper filers must submit an original and one copy of each filing (and additional copies if multiple dockets appear). All filings must be addressed to the Commission's Secretary. Specific postal and overnight mailing addresses are provided for paper submissions. Comments must be filed by the date stated in the DATES section (e.g., by February 3, 2026 for this document) and are identified by the docket number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition and limits on late filings in direct final proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid unwarranted delay in direct final rulemaking, filings addressing the rule changes are prohibited after a defined cut-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless further direction is published in the Federal Register, filings addressing the rule changes are prohibited more than 20 days after Federal Register publication; if a petition for reconsideration is filed, the Commission will address any comment process associated with such petition in light of the prohibition on filings addressing the rule changes more than 30 days after Federal Register publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: State EAS Plans — required elements
rubrics_metrics.description: State EAS Plans must include specific elements laid out in revised §11.21(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required elements include: (1) list of EAS header codes and messages (NP, LP, SP, SR); (2) procedures for state emergency management officials, NWS, and EAS Participant personnel to transmit emergency information and how state/local dissemination differs from National Emergency Message strategy; (3) procedures for state and local activations and list of authorized entities; (4) a monitoring assignment matrix (computer readable) showing monitoring assignments and primary/backup paths for the National Emergency Message, with CAP-specific aggregation/distribution details if applicable and notes about primary stations using program-originating boosters; (5) state procedures for special EAS tests and Required Monthly Tests (RMTs); (6) list of satellite-based communications resources used as alternate monitoring assignments; and (7) the SECC governance structure including duties, membership selection process, and administrative structure; (8) certification by the SECC Chairperson or Vice-Chairperson that the SECC met at least once in the prior 12 months before submitting the annual updated plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: State EAS Plan administration, approval, and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for administration and Commission review/approval of State EAS Plans as described in §11.21(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State EAS Plans are administered by State Emergency Communications Committees (SECC). The Commission encourages State chief executives to establish/review SECCs. Plans must be reviewed and approved by the Chief, Public Safety and Homeland Security Bureau prior to implementation to ensure consistency with national plans, FCC regulations, and EAS operation. The Bureau will review and approve plans, including annual updated plans, within 60 days of receipt provided no defects are found. If a plan is defective, the SECC will be notified of required corrections; a corrected plan may be resubmitted and restarts the 60-day review period. Approval dates will be listed on the Commission's website.

rubrics_metrics.name: State EAS Plans — annual update requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: State EAS Plans must be updated on an annual basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section §11.21(b) requires State EAS Plans to be updated annually and to include the enumerated elements; the SECC must certify it met at least once in the twelve months prior to submitting the annual updated plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual certification requirement for covered 911 service providers
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered 911 service providers must submit an annual certification to the Commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revised §9.19(c) provides: 'On October 15 of each year, a certifying official of every covered 911 service provider shall submit a certification to the Commission as follows.' (The text indicates an annual October 15 certification obligation for covered providers.)
